items.followUp: What are intermolecular forces? Give one example involving water molecules.

rubric.why: The definition identifies the forces and the particles between which they act.
rubric.description: Defines intermolecular forces as attractive forces between molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they are attractive forces between molecules; accept equivalent wording such as forces of attraction among molecules.

rubric.why: An example demonstrates a specific intermolecular force.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid example.

modelAnswer: Intermolecular forces are the forces of attraction between molecules.
Hydrogen bonding between water molecules is an example.

items.followUp: Explain why the density of a gas increases when it is cooled.

rubric.why: Cooling makes a gas occupy less volume under the same pressure.
rubric.description: States that a gas contracts or its volume decreases on cooling.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the decrease in volume.

rubric.why: For a fixed mass, reducing volume increases density (density = mass/volume).
rubric.description: Connects the reduced volume to an increase in density.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that density increases because the same mass occupies less volume.

modelAnswer: On cooling, a gas contracts and its volume decreases (at constant pressure).
Since density = mass/volume and the mass remains constant, the density increases.

items.followUp: Define allotropy and name two allotropes of carbon.

rubric.why: Allotropy describes the occurrence of an element in multiple forms.
rubric.description: Defines allotropy as the existence of an element in two or more different forms in the same physical state.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the same element exists in different forms; the same physical state may be included.

rubric.why: A valid example shows an element that has different allotropic forms.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as diamond and graphite as forms of carbon.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example of allotropy.

modelAnswer: Allotropy is the property of an element to exist in two or more different forms in the same physical state.
Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon.

items.followUp: How can the Tyndall effect be used to distinguish a colloidal solution from a true solution?

rubric.why: Colloidal particles scatter a beam of light.
rubric.description: Describes shining a beam of light through the sample and observing scattering (the Tyndall effect).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the light-scattering test.

rubric.why: The comparison with a true solution confirms whether the sample is colloidal.
rubric.description: States that a colloid scatters the light, whereas a true solution does not.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct observation distinguishing the two.

modelAnswer: Pass a narrow beam of light through the given solution in a dark room.
A colloidal solution scatters the light (Tyndall effect), while a true solution does not.

items.followUp: Why does oil not mix with water?

rubric.why: Benzene is non-polar, unlike polar water.
rubric.description: Identifies benzene as non-polar and water as polar.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the difference in polarity.

rubric.why: Polar and non-polar substances do not attract sufficiently to mix; substances of similar polarity dissolve one another.
rubric.description: Explains that benzene is insoluble because polar water does not dissolve non-polar benzene.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the solubility explanation, including the like-dissolves-like principle.

modelAnswer: Benzene is non-polar, whereas water is polar.
Polar water does not dissolve non-polar benzene; substances with similar polarity dissolve in one another.

items.followUp: Define a solute and give an example from salt water.

rubric.why: The definition describes the role of the solvent in a solution.
rubric.description: Defines a solvent as the substance in which the solute dissolves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: A correct example identifies a solvent in a solution.
rubric.description: Gives water as the solvent in a salt solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example.

modelAnswer: A solvent is the substance in which a solute dissolves.
Water is the solvent in a salt solution.

items.followUp: Write two examples of strong electrolytes.

rubric.why: Acetic acid and ammonium hydroxide are examples of weak electrolytes.
rubric.description: Gives one correct example of a weak electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid example.

rubric.why: A second correct example completes the requested pair.
rubric.description: Gives a second correct example of a weak electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another valid example; do not award both marks for only one example.

items.followUp: Write two physical properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: Metals possess several characteristic physical properties.
rubric.description: Gives one physical property of metals, such as lustre, malleability, ductility, conductivity, or sonority.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct physical property.

rubric.why: A second distinct property is required for the full answer.
rubric.description: Gives a second distinct physical property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another correct physical property.
